options: Every possible pair of values of any two parameters appears in at least one test
Every possible combination of all parameters is tested
Every parameter is tested with one value
Every test uses two parameters only
questions.explanation: Pairwise coverage needs each value pair for each parameter pair. All combinations is exhaustive testing, one value per parameter is much weaker, and tests still set every parameter.

questions.prompt: Three parameters each have 2 values. How many exhaustive combinations exist?
questions.explanation: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. Pairwise can cover all pairs here with 4 tests, which is the point of the technique.

questions.prompt: The minimum number of pairwise tests is at least the product of the two largest parameter value counts.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Every pair of values from the two largest parameters must appear, and each test covers only one such pair, so the product is a lower bound.

questions.prompt: Parameters: browser (4 values), OS (3), language (5), payment (2). What is the lower bound on pairwise tests?
questions.explanation: The two largest parameters are language (5) and browser (4), giving 5 x 4 = 20 pairs that each need a test. 120 is exhaustive, 14 is the sum of all values, and 5 is only the largest parameter.

questions.prompt: Which situations make pairwise testing a good choice? Select all that apply.
options: Many configuration options that interact
A tight schedule where exhaustive combinations are impossible
Evidence that most defects involve one or two interacting factors
A single input field with one valid range
questions.explanation: Pairwise shines when many parameters combine and time is limited, and it relies on the observation that most interaction defects involve few factors. A single range is better handled by EP and BVA.

questions.prompt: A generated pairwise set includes the combination OS = iOS with browser = Edge for Mac, which cannot exist. What should you do?
options: Declare the constraint in the tool so it generates a valid set, rather than deleting rows afterwards
Delete the row and keep the rest unchanged
Run the impossible test anyway
Abandon pairwise testing
questions.explanation: Deleting rows can silently remove other valid pairs that only appeared in that row. Modern tools support constraints so the set stays complete over valid combinations. Running impossible tests wastes time, and one constraint does not invalidate the technique.

questions.prompt: A defect occurs only when currency = JPY, payment = Wallet and country = Brazil all occur together. Will a pairwise set reliably find it?
options: No; pairwise guarantees only pairs, so this triple might not appear. Use 3-wise coverage for high-risk parameters
Yes; pairwise covers all triples too
Yes, because Brazil appears in at least one test
No, combinatorial testing never finds such defects
questions.explanation: Pairwise covers every pair, not every triple. Higher-strength (t-wise) coverage can be applied where interactions of three factors are a known risk.

questions.prompt: Your pairwise set for a booking form has 12 tests. All pass, but production users fail when using a value the tester never included: country = 'Other'. What was the main weakness?
options: The parameter values chosen for the model were incomplete; pairwise only combines the values you give it, so EP and risk analysis must pick values first
Pairwise should have used more tests per pair
The tool generated wrong pairs
Pairwise cannot handle text values
questions.explanation: Combinatorial tools are only as good as the model. If a value class is missing, no combination includes it. Choosing values with EP, BVA and risk analysis comes first.

questions.prompt: There are 3 parameters with values A: {a1, a2}, B: {b1, b2}, C: {c1, c2}. A tester proposes: (a1,b1,c1), (a1,b2,c2), (a2,b1,c2), (a2,b2,c1). Is this a complete pairwise set?
options: Yes; every pair for A-B, A-C and B-C appears exactly once
No; (a1, c2) is missing
No; (b2, c1) is missing
No; pairwise needs all 8 combinations
questions.explanation: A-B pairs: a1b1, a1b2, a2b1, a2b2. A-C: a1c1, a1c2, a2c2, a2c1. B-C: b1c1, b2c2, b1c2, b2c1. All 12 pairs are present in 4 tests, the classic orthogonal array. The claimed missing pairs are actually in rows 2 and 4.

coding.title: Exhaustive count and pairwise lower bound
coding.prompt:
Write `combo_stats(params)` where `params` maps each parameter name to its list of values. Return a tuple `(exhaustive, lower_bound)`: the number of exhaustive combinations, and the pairwise lower bound (product of the two largest value counts). With a single parameter, the lower bound is its value count.

Example: `combo_stats({'browser': ['c', 'f', 's', 'e'], 'os': ['w', 'm', 'l'], 'lang': ['en', 'de']})` returns `(24, 12)`.
coding.solution:
import math

def combo_stats(params):
    sizes = sorted((len(v) for v in params.values()), reverse=True)
    exhaustive = math.prod(sizes)
    lower = sizes[0] * sizes[1] if len(sizes) > 1 else sizes[0]
    return exhaustive, lower
coding.explanation: The exhaustive count is the product of all value counts. Every pair of values from the two biggest parameters must appear in a different test, so their product is a lower bound for pairwise.
hints: Get the list of value counts and sort it descending.

tests.name: Four parameters
tests.code:
p = {'a': list(range(4)), 'b': list(range(3)), 'c': list(range(5)), 'd': list(range(2))}
assert combo_stats(p) == (120, 20), combo_stats(p)

coding.title: Find missing pairs in a test set
coding.prompt:
Write `missing_pairs(params, tests)` where `params` maps parameter names to value lists and `tests` is a list of dicts (one value per parameter). Return a **sorted list** of tuples `(p1, v1, p2, v2)` for every value pair not covered by any test, considering parameter pairs with `p1 < p2` alphabetically.

Example: with `{'a': [1, 2], 'b': ['x', 'y']}` and tests `[{'a': 1, 'b': 'x'}, {'a': 2, 'b': 'y'}]`, the result is `[('a', 1, 'b', 'y'), ('a', 2, 'b', 'x')]`.
coding.explanation: For each pair of parameters, collect the value pairs the tests actually cover, then compare with every required pair. This is how you check a hand-made or edited pairwise set, for example after removing rows for constraints.
hints: Build a set of covered (t[p1], t[p2]) for each pair.
Report every (v1, v2) not in the set.

coding.title: Generate a pairwise set greedily
coding.prompt:
Write `pairwise(params)` returning a list of test dicts that covers **every value pair** of every two parameters. Use a simple greedy approach: repeatedly pick, from all exhaustive combinations, the one that covers the most still-uncovered pairs, until none remain. Iterate combinations in `itertools.product` order over parameters in **dict order**, and pick the first one on ties.

The tests check that your set is complete and small: for 4 parameters of 3 values each it must have **at most 11** tests (exhaustive would be 81).
coding.explanation: The greedy algorithm always adds the combination that covers the most uncovered pairs, so coverage grows quickly and the loop stops when every pair is covered. Real tools (such as PICT) use smarter heuristics and support constraints, but the idea is the same. `max` returns the first maximal element, which gives the deterministic tie-break.
hints: Represent a covered pair as (param1, value1, param2, value2).
The set of all required pairs is the union of pairs over all exhaustive combinations.
Loop: choose `max(candidates, key=new pairs covered)`, add it, remove its pairs.

tests.name: Covers every pair
Much smaller than exhaustive
Two parameters need all combinations

T = pairwise({'a': [1, 2], 'b': [1, 2, 3]})
assert len(T) == 6 and len({(t['a'], t['b']) for t in T}) == 6
